enriched_description: Spiderlike arachnid measuring 5-10 mm in body length with extremely long, slender legs spanning 30-50 mm. Body is small, rounded, and compact with a fused cephalothorax and abdomen (unlike spiders, the body segments are broadly joined without a narrow waist). Body coloration is dark brown to black with a smooth, glossy surface. The most distinctive feature is the eight extremely elongated, thread-like legs; legs are disproportionately long relative to body size, with the second pair of legs being the longest and used as sensory organs. Legs are smooth and unsegmented in appearance. Head has a single pair of eyes positioned dorsally on a small turret (ocularium). No silk-producing glands or fangs; mouthparts are small chelicerae used for chewing. The harvestman exhibits a characteristic posture with body elevated on extended legs, creating a spider-like silhouette. Movement is slow and deliberate.

Arachnid measuring 5-20 cm in total length with a distinctive body plan consisting of a cephalothorax (prosoma) and segmented abdomen (opisthosoma). Body coloration is yellow-brown to black with a smooth, glossy exoskeleton. Cephalothorax bears a pair of large, pincer-like pedipalps (claws) at the anterior end; pedipalps are robust and heavily sclerotized with spiny inner margins. Four pairs of walking legs extend from the cephalothorax; legs are slender with terminal claws. The most distinctive feature is the elongated, segmented tail (metasoma) comprising five segments ending in a bulbous telson (stinger) containing venom glands; tail curves upward and forward over the back in a characteristic defensive posture. Body surface is smooth with fine granular texture. Scorpions fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The scorpion exhibits a characteristic walking posture with pedipalps held forward and tail curved overhead.

Large orb-weaving spider measuring 20-28 mm in body length (females) with distinctive black and yellow coloration. Cephalothorax (front body segment) is covered in dense silver-white hairs creating a silvery appearance. Abdomen (rear body segment) is large and oval with a striking pattern: black background with four to five pairs of yellow spots arranged symmetrically; the yellow spots are bright and contrasting. Legs are long and banded with alternating black and yellow rings; legs are covered in fine spines. The spider constructs a large, circular orb web (30-60 cm diameter) with a distinctive zigzag stabilimentum (silk decoration) running vertically through the center of the web. The spider hangs head-down in the center of the web with legs spread radially. Eyes are small and arranged in two rows. The spider exhibits a characteristic stationary posture in the web center, waiting for prey.

Medium-sized orb-weaving spider measuring 15-20 mm in body length (females) with orange and tan coloration. Cephalothorax is yellowish-brown with a distinct white longitudinal stripe running down the midline. Abdomen is large and oval with a mottled pattern of orange, tan, and brown; the dorsal surface has a leaf-like marking in darker brown. Legs are long and banded with alternating dark and light rings; legs are covered in fine spines and hairs. The spider constructs a large, circular orb web (30-50 cm diameter) typically in sheltered locations such as barns, eaves, or window frames. The web is rebuilt daily, with the old web consumed and recycled. The spider hangs head-down in the center of the web with legs spread radially. Eyes are small and arranged in two rows. The spider exhibits a characteristic stationary posture in the web center.

Medium-sized orb-weaving spider measuring 12-18 mm in body length (females) with distinctive cross-shaped marking on the abdomen. Cephalothorax is brownish-grey with fine hairs. Abdomen is large and oval with a dark brown background and a prominent white or cream-colored cross-shaped marking (crucifix pattern) on the dorsal surface; the cross is formed by intersecting bands creating a distinctive cruciform shape. Legs are long and banded with alternating dark and light rings; legs are covered in fine spines. The spider constructs a large, circular orb web (30-60 cm diameter) typically in gardens, hedgerows, or between branches. The web often includes a zigzag stabilimentum (silk decoration) running vertically through the center. The spider hangs head-down in the center of the web with legs spread radially. Eyes are small and arranged in two rows. The spider exhibits a characteristic stationary posture in the web center.

Venomous spider measuring 8-14 mm in body length (females) with glossy black coloration and distinctive red marking. Body is entirely jet black with a smooth, highly glossy, almost lacquered appearance. The most distinctive feature is the bright red hourglass-shaped marking on the ventral (underside) surface of the abdomen; the hourglass consists of two triangular red patches connected at the apex, creating a symmetrical hourglass shape. Some individuals have additional red spots on the dorsal surface of the abdomen. Cephalothorax is small and black. Legs are long, slender, and uniformly black without banding; legs are smooth without spines. The spider constructs an irregular, tangled web close to the ground in dark, sheltered locations. The female exhibits a characteristic posture hanging upside-down in the web with legs drawn close to the body. Males are much smaller (3-4 mm) and lack the distinctive marking.

Large mygalomorph spider measuring 5-12 cm in body length with a massive, heavily-built body covered in dense hair. Body coloration varies by species: common colors include black, brown, grey, or iridescent blue-green. Cephalothorax is large and robust, covered in dense, velvety hairs. Abdomen is large and oval, also covered in dense hair; some species have urticating (irritating) hairs on the abdomen that can be flicked at predators. The most distinctive feature is the dense covering of long, bristly hairs (setae) over the entire body and legs, creating a furry, hairy appearance. Legs are thick and robust with eight eyes arranged in a compact group at the front of the cephalothorax. Chelicerae (fangs) are large and prominent, projecting downward. The tarantula exhibits a characteristic slow, deliberate walking posture with body held close to the ground. Many species are terrestrial burrowers.

Medium to large hunting spider measuring 10-35 mm in body length with robust, hairy body adapted for ground hunting. Body coloration is grey, brown, or black with longitudinal stripes or mottled patterning providing camouflage against ground surfaces. Cephalothorax is broad and flat with a distinct longitudinal stripe running down the midline. Abdomen is oval and covered in dense hairs with variable patterning. The most distinctive feature is the eye arrangement: eight eyes arranged in three rows (four small eyes in the front row, two large eyes in the middle row, and two medium eyes in the back row); the two large median eyes are prominent and forward-facing, providing excellent vision for hunting. Legs are long and robust, covered in spines and hairs, adapted for rapid running. The wolf spider does not construct a web; it hunts by actively pursuing prey on the ground. The spider exhibits a characteristic alert posture with legs spread and body elevated, ready for rapid movement.

Small parasitic arachnid measuring 2-10 mm in body length (unfed) with a flattened, oval body adapted for blood-feeding. Body coloration is reddish-brown to dark brown with a smooth, leathery exoskeleton. The most distinctive feature is the barbed proboscis (hypostome) projecting from the anterior end, used for attaching to hosts; the proboscis is covered in backward-pointing barbs that anchor the tick during feeding. Body is dorsoventrally flattened when unfed, becoming engorged and spherical after feeding (expanding to 10x original size). Cephalothorax and abdomen are fused into a single body unit (idiosoma) without visible segmentation. Legs are short and stout with eight legs in adults (six in larvae); legs terminate in claws and adhesive pads for clinging to hosts. The tick exhibits a characteristic questing posture, perched on vegetation with front legs extended, waiting to latch onto passing hosts.

Predatory arthropod measuring 10-30 cm in total length with a flattened, segmented body bearing one pair of legs per segment. Body coloration is yellow-brown to reddish-brown with a smooth, glossy exoskeleton. The body consists of 15-173 segments (depending on species), each bearing a single pair of legs; legs are long and slender, extending laterally from the body. The most distinctive feature is the modified first pair of legs (forcipules) transformed into venomous claws (poison claws) located beneath the head; forcipules are large, curved, and used to capture and immobilize prey. Head is flattened with a pair of long, segmented antennae extending forward; eyes are small or absent. The centipede exhibits a characteristic rapid, undulating running motion with legs moving in coordinated waves. Body is dorsoventrally flattened. The last pair of legs is often elongated and held backward, resembling antennae.
